title: UNIT 7: NUCLEAR PHYSICS
notes:
✓ Nuclear physics → Studies the atomic nucleus, its constituents, nuclear forces, nuclear stability, radioactivity, nuclear reactions, fission, fusion, nuclear energy, nuclear medicine and radiation safety.

◆ CORE IDEA
✓ Nucleus → Contains protons and neutrons.
✓ Nuclear force → Binds nucleons together.
✓ Radioactivity → Spontaneous decay of unstable nuclei.
✓ Fission → Heavy nucleus splits.
✓ Fusion → Light nuclei combine.
✓ Mass–energy equivalence → Mass can be converted into energy:
E = mc²

title: 7.1 THE NUCLEUS
notes:
✓ Nucleus → The tiny, dense central region of an atom containing almost all of its mass and all of its positive charge.

◆ NUCLEONS
✓ Proton → Positive charge, approximately 1 u mass.
✓ Neutron → No electric charge, approximately 1 u mass.
✓ Proton + neutron → Nucleons.

✓ Electrons → Occupy the region outside the nucleus.

◆ NUCLEAR NOTATION
✓ An atom is represented as:
ᴬZX

✓ Z → Atomic number = number of protons.
✓ A → Mass number = number of protons + neutrons.
✓ N → Number of neutrons:
N = A − Z

◆ NUCLEAR SIZE
✓ Approximate nuclear radius:
R = R₀A¹ᐟ³

✓ R₀ ≈ 1.2 × 10⁻¹⁵ m = 1.2 fm.

✓ The nucleus → Is extremely small compared with the atom; most of the atom is empty space.

◆ ISOTOPES
✓ Isotopes → Atoms of the same element having the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.

◆ Examples → ¹²₆C, ¹³₆C and ¹⁴₆C.

◆ DISCOVERY OF THE NUCLEUS
✓ Rutherford’s α-particle scattering experiment showed that:

✓ Most α-particles passed through the gold foil → Most of the atom is empty space.

✓ Some were slightly deflected → Positive charge is concentrated in a small region.

✓ Very few were strongly deflected or reflected → The nucleus is tiny, dense and contains most of the atomic mass and positive charge.

◆ NUCLEAR FORCES
✓ Strong nuclear force → Very strong, short-range attractive force between nucleons; it holds the nucleus together despite proton–proton electrical repulsion.

✓ Weak nuclear force → Extremely short-range force involved in processes such as beta decay.

✓ Key idea → A stable nucleus results from the balance between attractive nuclear forces and repulsive electrostatic forces between protons.

title: 7.1.1 NUCLEAR MASS, MASS DEFECT & BINDING ENERGY
notes:
✓ Mass defect → The difference between the measured mass of a nucleus and the combined masses of its separated protons and neutrons.

◆ MASS DEFECT
✓ Δm = Zmp + (A − Z)mn − M

✓ mp → Proton mass.
✓ mn → Neutron mass.
✓ M → Nuclear mass.

◆ MASS–ENERGY EQUIVALENCE
✓ Mass defect → Corresponds to binding energy:
BE = Δmc²

✓ If Δm is measured in atomic mass units (u):
BE(MeV) = Δm × 931.1 MeV

◆ NUCLEAR BINDING ENERGY
✓ Binding energy → Energy required to completely separate a nucleus into its individual nucleons.

✓ Binding energy → Also the energy released when the nucleus forms from its nucleons.

◆ BINDING ENERGY PER NUCLEON
✓ BEN = BE/A

✓ Larger binding energy per nucleon → Generally indicates greater nuclear stability.

◆ NUCLEAR STABILITY
✓ Nuclei with an appropriate balance of protons and neutrons → Are more stable.

✓ Very heavy nuclei → Can become unstable because electrostatic repulsion between their many protons becomes increasingly important.

✓ Mass defect → “Missing” mass converted into binding energy.
✓ Binding energy → Energy holding the nucleus together.
✓ Binding energy per nucleon → Useful measure for comparing nuclear stability.

title: 7.2 RADIOACTIVITY
notes:
✓ Radioactivity → The spontaneous disintegration of unstable atomic nuclei into more stable nuclei, accompanied by the emission of radiation and energy.

✓ Radioactive decay → Is spontaneous and statistically random for individual nuclei.

◆ ALPHA (α) DECAY
✓ α-particle → A helium nucleus:
⁴₂He

✓ General reaction:
ᴬZX → ᴬ⁻⁴Z⁻²Y + ⁴₂He

✓ Mass number → Decreases by 4.
✓ Atomic number → Decreases by 2.

◆ BETA-MINUS (β⁻) DECAY
✓ A neutron → Changes into a proton while emitting an electron and an antineutrino:
n → p + e⁻ + ν̄

✓ General nuclear change:
ᴬZX → ᴬZ+1Y + β⁻ + ν̄

✓ Mass number → Remains unchanged.
✓ Atomic number → Increases by 1.

◆ BETA-PLUS (β⁺) DECAY
✓ A proton → Changes into a neutron while emitting a positron and a neutrino:
p → n + e⁺ + ν

✓ General nuclear change:
ᴬZX → ᴬZ−1Y + β⁺ + ν

✓ Mass number → Remains unchanged.
✓ Atomic number → Decreases by 1.

◆ GAMMA (γ) RADIATION
✓ Gamma rays → High-energy, high-frequency electromagnetic radiation emitted when an excited nucleus loses excess energy.

✓ Gamma emission → No change in A or Z.

◆ PENETRATION & IONIZATION
✓ α → High ionizing power, low penetration.
✓ β → Medium ionizing power and penetration.
✓ γ → Very high penetration, lower ionizing power than α.

✓ Key idea → α changes both A and Z; β changes Z only; γ changes neither A nor Z.

title: 7.2.1 RADIOACTIVE DECAY LAW, ACTIVITY & HALF-LIFE
notes:
✓ Radioactive decay → Follows an exponential law.

◆ DECAY EQUATION
✓ N(t) = N₀e⁻λt

✓ N₀ → Initial number of radioactive nuclei.
✓ N(t) → Number remaining after time t.
✓ λ → Decay constant.

◆ DECAY CONSTANT
✓ λ → Probability of decay per unit time for a radioactive nucleus.
✓ Unit → s⁻¹.

◆ ACTIVITY
✓ Activity → Rate at which radioactive nuclei decay:
A = −ΔN/Δt

✓ For radioactive decay:
A = λN

✓ Unit → becquerel (Bq).
✓ 1 Bq = 1 decay/s.

✓ Another unit → curie.
✓ 1 Ci = 3.7 × 10¹⁰ Bq.

◆ HALF-LIFE
✓ Half-life, t₁/₂ → Time required for half of the original radioactive nuclei to decay, or for the amount remaining to become half its initial value.

✓ After one half-life:
N = N₀/2

✓ Relationship:
t₁/₂ = ln2/λ = 0.693/λ

✓ After n half-lives:
N = N₀(½)ⁿ

✓ Half-life → Is constant for a particular radioisotope and does not depend on the initial amount of the sample.

✓ Radioactive decay → Is random for an individual nucleus, but predictable statistically for a large sample.

title: 7.2.2 RADIATION DOSE, DETECTION & HAZARDS
notes:
✓ Nuclear radiation → Can ionize atoms and molecules by removing electrons.

✓ Excessive exposure → Can damage cells and living tissues.

◆ ABSORBED DOSE
✓ Absorbed dose → Energy deposited by radiation per unit mass:
D = E/m

✓ SI unit → gray (Gy).
✓ 1 Gy = 1 J/kg.
✓ Another unit → rad.
✓ 1 rad = 0.01 Gy.

◆ RADIATION DETECTORS
✓ Scintillator → Detects radiation through flashes of light produced in a scintillating material.
✓ Gaseous ionization detector → Detects ionization produced in a gas.
✓ Geiger–Müller counter → Detects ionizing radiation through electrical pulses produced by ionization in a gas-filled tube.

◆ PENETRATION
✓ Alpha → Stopped relatively easily by thin materials.
✓ Beta → Can be reduced/stopped by materials such as aluminum.
✓ Gamma → Highly penetrating; denser shielding such as lead is required.

◆ RADIATION HAZARDS
✓ Ionizing radiation → Can damage living tissue.

✓ Severity → Depends on factors such as radiation type, dose and exposure conditions.

◆ PROTECTION PRINCIPLES
✓ Reduce exposure time → Less dose.
✓ Increase distance from source → Lower exposure.
✓ Use appropriate shielding → Reduces radiation reaching the body.
✓ Follow controlled procedures → When handling radioactive materials.

title: 7.3 USE OF NUCLEAR RADIATION
notes:
✓ Nuclear radiation → Has useful applications in medicine, radioactive dating, agriculture, industry and energy production.

✓ Nuclear medicine → Includes medical applications of radioactive materials for diagnosis and treatment.

◆ NUCLEAR MEDICINE
✓ Radioisotopes → Can be used for diagnosis and treatment.

◆ DIAGNOSIS
✓ Radioactive tracer → Can be introduced into the body and its emitted radiation detected to provide information about the functioning of organs.

✓ Technetium-99 → An important radioisotope used in medical investigations.

◆ TREATMENT
✓ Radiation → Can be directed or delivered to diseased tissue to destroy abnormal cells.

✓ Radioactive materials → Are used in treatments such as those involving thyroid disorders and cancer.

◆ RADIOACTIVE DATING
✓ Radioactive decay → Can be used to estimate the age of materials containing a suitable radioisotope.

✓ Carbon-14 dating → Is used for determining the age of once-living materials.

✓ As radioactive nuclei decay → The amount of the parent isotope decreases according to the decay law.

◆ NUCLEAR ENERGY
✓ Nuclear reactions → Release very large amounts of energy because small changes in mass correspond to large energy changes through:
E = mc²

◆ OTHER APPLICATIONS
Agriculture
Industry
Medicine
Water and sanitation
Power generation

✓ Key idea → The same radiation that can be hazardous when uncontrolled can be extremely useful when carefully controlled.

title: 7.4 NUCLEAR REACTIONS
notes:
✓ Nuclear reaction → A process in which an atomic nucleus interacts with another particle or nucleus and changes into different nuclei or particles.

✓ Nuclear equations must conserve:
◆ Mass number (A)
◆ Atomic number (Z)
◆ Energy and momentum

◆ NUCLEAR FISSION
✓ Fission → Occurs when a heavy nucleus splits into two or more smaller nuclei, usually after absorbing a neutron.

✓ Example:
²³⁵₉₂U + ¹₀n → ¹⁴⁴₅₆Ba + ⁸⁹₃₆Kr + 3¹₀n + energy

✓ Large amounts of energy → Are released because the products have greater binding energy per nucleon than the original heavy nucleus.

◆ CHAIN REACTION
✓ Neutrons released during fission → Can cause additional fissions.

✓ Chain reaction → Occurs if each fission produces enough subsequent fissions.

✓ Controlled chain reaction → Used in nuclear reactors.
✓ Uncontrolled chain reaction → Can release energy extremely rapidly.

◆ NUCLEAR REACTORS
✓ Nuclear reactor → Provides controlled nuclear fission to produce useful energy.

◆ Important reactor concepts:
✓ Fuel → Contains fissionable material.
✓ Moderator → Slows neutrons so they can efficiently cause further fission.
✓ Control rods → Absorb neutrons and regulate the chain reaction.
✓ Coolant → Removes heat from the reactor core.

◆ POWER REACTOR
✓ Produces useful thermal energy → Can ultimately be converted into electrical energy.

◆ RESEARCH REACTOR
✓ Designed mainly for research, isotope production, training and other scientific applications rather than large-scale electricity generation.

◆ FISSION APPLICATIONS
Electricity generation
Production of radioisotopes
Research
Nuclear medicine

◆ NUCLEAR WASTE
✓ Fission → Produces radioactive waste that requires careful handling, storage and disposal because some radioactive products remain hazardous for long periods.

title: 7.4.1 NUCLEAR FUSION REACTION & ITS USES
notes:
✓ Nuclear fusion → Occurs when two or more light nuclei combine to form a heavier nucleus and release energy.

◆ FUSION IN STARS
✓ The Sun and other stars → Produce enormous energy through nuclear fusion involving hydrogen nuclei.

✓ Simplified representation:
4¹₁H → ⁴₂He + energy + other products

✓ Decrease in mass → Is converted into energy according to:
E = mc²

◆ CONDITIONS FOR FUSION
✓ Very high temperature → Required so that positively charged nuclei have enough kinetic energy to overcome their electrostatic repulsion and collide.

✓ High density/confinement → Helps maintain the conditions needed for fusion.

◆ HYDROGEN ISOTOPES
✓ Deuterium → ²₁H.
✓ Tritium → ³₁H.

✓ Deuterium–tritium fusion reaction:
²₁H + ³₁H → ⁴₂He + ¹₀n + energy

◆ ADVANTAGES OF FUSION
Very large energy release
Hydrogen isotopes can serve as fuel
Fusion is the energy source of stars

◆ FISSION vs FUSION
✓ Fission → Heavy nucleus splits.
✓ Fusion → Light nuclei combine.
✓ Fission → Chain reactions can occur.
✓ Fusion → Requires extremely high temperatures and suitable confinement.

✓ Both processes → Release nuclear energy through changes in nuclear binding energy.

title: 7.5 SAFETY RULES AGAINST HAZARDS OF NUCLEAR RADIATION
notes:
✓ Radiation safety → Aims to minimize unnecessary exposure to ionizing radiation and protect people, equipment and the environment.

◆ TIME
✓ Minimize the time spent near a radiation source → Less exposure time means smaller radiation dose.

◆ DISTANCE
✓ Increase the distance from the radiation source whenever possible → Greater distance generally reduces exposure.

◆ SHIELDING
✓ Use appropriate shielding between the source and the person.

✓ Examples → Suitable materials such as lead, concrete or other approved shielding depending on the radiation type and energy.

◆ SAFE HANDLING
✓ Never handle radioactive materials unnecessarily.
✓ Follow approved laboratory and medical procedures.
✓ Use appropriate protective equipment.
✓ Keep radioactive sources properly labeled and secured.
✓ Do not eat or drink while handling radioactive materials.
✓ Wash hands after work involving radioactive materials.
✓ Keep radioactive sources away from the body and eyes.

◆ NUCLEAR WASTE
✓ Radioactive waste → Must be properly collected, contained, stored, monitored and disposed of according to safety procedures.

◆ NUCLEAR FACILITY SAFETY
✓ Safe handling and storage of radioactive materials.
✓ Control of exposure.
✓ Safe operation of nuclear facilities.
✓ Monitoring radiation levels.
✓ Emergency planning.
✓ Proper management of nuclear waste.

✓ GOLDEN RULE
Radiation protection → Minimize TIME + maximize DISTANCE + use appropriate SHIELDING.
